strengths: Addresses genuine limitations of existing benchmarks with well-motivated solutions (false positives, external dependencies, coarse metrics)
Exceptional data curation: 403 problems from official Olympiads with ~60 expert-designed test cases per problem and detailed quality assurance procedures
Comprehensive evaluation framework: 32 models, multiple complementary metrics (pass rate, percentile, medals, ELO), and direct human-model comparison
Rigorous dataset construction with multiple data sources, fallback strategies, and extensive documentation enabling reproducibility
Systematic empirical analysis including algorithm-specific performance, temporal contamination checking, reasoning trace categorization, and inference-time scaling
Self-contained offline evaluation system eliminating external API dependencies and enabling easy reproduction
Novel insights into reasoning behavior: strong models prioritize analysis over exploration, identifying persistent challenges in DP/tree problems despite reasoning capabilities
Clear public commitment: planned data/code release and continuous updates from newly released problems
weaknesses: Reasoning trace annotation lacks rigor: uses GPT-OSS-120B for annotation (circular), reports no inter-annotator agreement or validation metrics, 5k token segmentation choice unjustified
Incomplete human performance data: only 46 of 72 contests have results (~36% missing), limiting percentile calculations and human-model comparison scope
Superficial contamination analysis: absence of sharp performance bumps is not conclusive; GPT-5's knowledge cutoff overlaps with benchmark period; lacks rigorous similarity-based detection
Limited depth on algorithmic failures: identifies DP/tree problems as hard but provides surface-level explanations; hypothesis about 'creative observations' unsupported
Runtime error analysis unsupported: hypothesis that stronger models use aggressive optimizations lacks evidence; no examination of actual failing code or systematic error analysis
Concurrent work not thoroughly compared: acknowledges LiveCodeBench Pro, HLCE, OI-Bench, AetherCode but provides only qualitative comparisons, missing quantitative analysis
Difficulty ratings rely on user-generated sources (solved.ac/Luogu) not official ratings; LLM-inferred missing tags could introduce bias; no sensitivity analysis
Inference-time scaling analysis shallow: Pass@k and sequential scaling confirm expected patterns but lack practical guidance on token efficiency trade-offs
Missing elements: no inter-rater validation of annotations, limited discussion of geographic bias and ethical considerations, no ablation studies on design choices

Presentation issues: 38-page paper with redundancy; Figure 1 has overlapping labels; some design choices (e.g., 8 candidate solutions) lack justification; missing practical guidance for model developers

strengths: Substantial dataset engineering effort with rigorous validation: 403 problems from 14 official Olympiads, expert-curated test cases (avg. 60/problem) addressing false-positive issues in prior benchmarks
Comprehensive benchmarking of 32 LLMs across multiple categories with diverse evaluation metrics (pass rate, percentile, medals, ELO rating)
Practical contributions: self-contained offline evaluation system, integration of official human contestant rankings, planned public release, promise of continuous updates
Rigorous dataset construction and validation procedures with clear methodology; no evidence of temporal contamination
Well-documented appendices with detailed competition information, model details, and construction methodology
weaknesses: Core research question ('Can LLMs beat top humans?') has unsurprising answer (82nd percentile vs. 90th+ for medals); insights are mostly confirmatory rather than novel

Critical methodological flaw in reasoning trace analysis (Section 5.2): Uses LLM-based annotation (Gemini-2.0-Flash) without human validation, inter-annotator agreement metrics, or reliability assessment; noisy labels undermine conclusions about strategic token allocation

Shallow analysis of key findings: Algorithm-specific weaknesses identified (DP: 47% vs. Implementation: 72%) but no investigation of causes; error patterns remain speculative; vague suggestions ('curriculum-driven fine-tuning') lack substantiation

Limited novelty relative to concurrent work (LiveCodeBench-Pro, HLCE, OI-Bench): distinguishing feature (offline evaluation) is practical but not deeply innovative; unclear why practitioners should prefer LiveOIBench

Human percentile calculation concerns: Some contests have very few matched contestants (5-70 subjects); Codeforces rating matching via Google Search is error-prone; filtering reduces sample sizes further
No actionable insights or novel methods for addressing identified weaknesses; no investigation of why models fail on specific problem types; suggestions remain vague and unvalidated
Paper attempts too much: sprawls across dataset creation, benchmarking, algorithm-specific analysis, reasoning traces, error patterns, and scaling—lacking sufficient depth in any single dimension
Causal claims unjustified: 'High-performing models allocate reasoning tokens strategically' based on noisy LLM annotations; direction of causality unclear; no validation of annotation quality

strengths: Addresses critical limitations in existing coding benchmarks by providing expert-curated test sets from official Olympiads, eliminating ~50% false-positive rates present in prior work
High-quality data curation with rigorous verification: 403 problems from 72 contests with average 60 expert-designed test cases per problem, including subtask rubrics
Comprehensive multi-metric evaluation framework (pass rate, human percentile, medal system, ELO rating) enabling nuanced assessment of model capabilities beyond simple pass rates
Practical offline evaluation system with self-contained judge eliminates API dependencies and improves reproducibility and accessibility
Extensive experimental evaluation of 32 models with multiple analytical perspectives: algorithm-specific performance, reasoning trace analysis, error patterns, and inference-time scaling

Detailed behavioral insights from reasoning trace analysis showing stronger models prioritize structured planning/analysis over excessive exploration; systematic weaknesses identified for specific algorithms (DP: ~47%, segment trees: ~56%)
Clear evidence of no data contamination through temporal analysis across quarters from Q4'22 to Q2'25
Well-written paper with clear motivation, sound methodology, comprehensive appendices, and accessible presentation; commitment to releasing data, code, and results
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a resource/dataset paper without novel algorithms or techniques; evaluation metrics are standard and mostly borrowed from prior work

Reasoning trace analysis relies on GPT-OSS-120B for annotation without inter-annotator agreement validation, proper quality assessment, or statistical significance testing; lacks rigorous methodology validation

Human baseline limitations: only 46 of 72 contests (38.9%) have contestant data; Codeforces rating matching uses unvalidated heuristics; small contestant pools introduce statistical noise; claim about 90th percentile threshold needs clarification

Insufficient data contamination analysis: quarterly trends don't conclusively rule out contamination; no direct contamination checking methods employed; models trained on 2023+ data could include training on benchmark problems
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: claims of advantages over LiveCodeBench-Pro, HLCE, OI-Bench, AetherCode appear subjective without rigorous quality comparisons of problems and test cases

Limited causal analysis of performance gaps: algorithm-specific weaknesses identified (e.g., DP, segment trees) but underlying causes (representation complexity, compositionality, reasoning depth) not deeply investigated
Experimental design concerns: Pass@8 choice unjustified; no sensitivity analysis; subtask scoring aggregation details unclear; ELO formula sensitivity unexplored

Reproducibility gaps: website URL masked in submission; implementation details incomplete (timeouts, inference settings, sample sizes for analyses); interactive problem protocol not fully described; external API dependencies remain
